meta.title: Cenote & Reef Diving in Tulum | Kay Diving — PADI Courses & Guided Dives
meta.description: Guided cenote and reef diving in Tulum, from a first try dive to PADI Open Water and Advanced. Hotel transport, equipment, cenote entrance and snacks included. From $80.

hero.lede: Kay Diving guides cenote and reef dives around Tulum — from a first breath underwater to a PADI certification. Our guides do not just take you down; they tell you the history of the place while you are in it.
hero.alt: A diver silhouetted against the turquoise glow of a Tulum cenote, among bare branches rising through the water

about.h2: Three quarters of our planet are water. Let's go and explore them together.
about.p1: At Kay Diving we are passionate about the Mayan underworld. Our guides will not only take you on a personalised experience, they will teach you about the magical history of this place. We also take pride in our responsibility towards the environment, making conscious decisions about the way we protect this beautiful planet.
about.p2: The Riviera Maya has some of the most beautiful diving sites in the world, and some very good dive centres. What we take special pride in is making the tour yours — so that you feel at home, and the day is built around you rather than around a schedule.
about.question: We send you a few questions before the dive. What you have done before, what you want out of the day, what makes you uneasy. It is the difference between a dive that suits you and a dive that merely happens.
about.plateAlt: A Kay Diving guide carrying a tank down to the water in Tulum
about.plateNote: PERSONALISED · every tour built around you

products.intro: Every price below already includes transport from your hotel, equipment, the cenote entrance fee, and snacks and water. There is nothing to add on the day except the balance.

level.open-water-plus: Open Water · Advanced for the deeper sites

discover-scuba.name: Discover Scuba
discover-scuba.text: Your first glimpse of the underwater world. Learn the basics of scuba, then go and explore an open-air cenote with crystal clear water. No certification, no previous experience — just a guide, shallow water and a very good morning.
discover-scuba.alt: The open, jungle-fringed surface of Casa Cenote near Tulum

reef-cenote.name: Reef & Cenote
reef-cenote.text: One day, both halves of what makes this coast worth diving: the reef off Tankah, then the fresh water of Casa Cenote. Salt and sweet, turtles and stalactites, in a single morning.
reef-cenote.alt: A green turtle swimming over coral on the reef off Tulum

cenote-diving.name: Cenote Diving
cenote-diving.text: Into some of the most beautiful flooded caverns in the world. Which cenotes you dive depends on what you have done before — we choose them once we know your level, and we say so honestly if a site is not yet for you.
cenote-diving.alt: A diver descending past bare branches in a Tulum cenote

advanced-ow.name: Advanced Open Water
advanced-ow.text: The next step: five specialty dives taking you to thirty metres, across Casa Cenote, Cenote El Pit and the Tankah reef. Learning materials included.
advanced-ow.alt: A diver near the surface of a Tulum cenote beside a rock wall

open-water.name: Open Water Course
open-water.tagline: Join the fun, become a certified diver.
open-water.text: The full PADI Open Water licence over five dives, between Casa Cenote and the Tankah reef. No previous experience needed. You leave with a certification that works anywhere in the world.
open-water.alt: A Kay Diving guide carrying a tank to the water

snorkel.name: Snorkel tour
snorkel.text: For anyone who wants a little adventure and a lot of calm. Three different cenotes across half a day, finishing at one of the best local taquerías in town. No experience needed, and no tank.
snorkel.alt: A cenote near Tulum seen from the bank, jungle reflected in still water

items.q: Do I need to be certified to dive here?
items.a: Not to start. Discover Scuba takes people who have never breathed underwater, and the snorkel tour needs nothing at all. For cenote diving and the reef you need an Open Water certification, and the deeper cenote sites need Advanced — we will tell you honestly which sites are open to you.

items.q: What is actually included in the price?
items.a: Transport from your hotel to the dive sites, high quality equipment, the cenote entrance fee, and snacks and water. Both courses also include the learning materials. Nothing else is added on the day beyond the balance of the price you saw.

items.q: How deep do the dives go?
items.a: The figures on each card are the planned depth for that course or tour: about 9 metres (30 ft) for Discover Scuba and the Open Water course, 18 metres (60 ft) for cenote diving, and 27 metres (90 ft) on the Advanced course. Beyond those, the deepest cenotes we dive reach 40 metres — Cenote El Pit keeps going well past the recreational limit — and we only take divers there who hold the certification for it. We will tell you honestly which sites are open to you.

items.q: What is the difference between cavern and cave diving?
items.a: Cavern diving stays inside the natural daylight zone, within reach of the entrance and always with a direct route to the surface. Cave diving goes beyond daylight and needs its own certification — a different qualification entirely, and not something an Open Water card covers.
Cenotes sit at roughly 24–25 °C every day of the year, and the reef is a little warmer. Wetsuits are part of the equipment we provide — tell us if you run cold.

Fresh rainwater floating on heavier salt water. The boundary between them refracts light, so swimming through it looks like the water has turned to oil or frosted glass — then it closes behind you and the view snaps back. It is one of the strangest things you will see underwater.

items.q: Why do you send questions before the dive?
items.a: Because a tour built around you is better than a tour built around a schedule. We want to know what you have done before, what you are hoping for, and what makes you uneasy — so the day fits, rather than merely happening.

items.q: When is the best time of year to come?
items.a: Cenotes are sheltered from wind and swell, so they dive well all year. Light beams in the cenotes are strongest around the middle of the day. Reef conditions are generally best in the spring and early summer.

footer.blurb: Guided cenote and reef diving and PADI courses in Tulum, Quintana Roo. Transport, equipment, cenote entrance and snacks included in every price.

thanks.p: Your deposit is in and the date is held. A guide will message you on WhatsApp within a few hours with the meeting point, the time, and the few questions we ask before every dive. The balance is settled on the day.

pending.p: Your bank or the payment method you chose has not confirmed yet — with OXXO or a transfer this can take a few hours. We hold the date meanwhile and write to you the moment it clears.

failed.p: Nothing was charged and no date is held. Cards issued outside Mexico are sometimes refused on a first attempt — try again, or write to us on WhatsApp and we will hold the date by hand.
